name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC advocacy group pushes for AAPI education, hate crime prevention
description: North Carolina Asian Americans Together organized the press conference as part of its annual Asian American Advocacy Day.
text:
Rep. Ya Liu (D-Wake) speaks about House Bill 835, "Learning AAPI Contributions in Schools," at a press conference on April 29, 2026. (Photo: Christine Zhu/NC Newsline)Lawmakers and local advocates called on the North Carolina General Assembly Wednesday to pass bills incorporating AAPI contributions into school curriculums and preventing hate crimes. 
North Carolina Asian Americans Together organized the press conference as part of its annual Asian American Advocacy Day.
There are more than 300,000 Asian Americans in North Carolina, according to Carolina Demography. Asian Americans are one of the fastest growing communities in the state and across the south.
Phuong Tran, communications director at NCAAT, said the group celebrated its 10th anniversary this year. It was founded to provide a voice in the state policy arena for the needs of Asian communities. 
“Too many people felt invisible, spoken about or to, but not with,” Tran said. “So we set out to change that, and over the past decade, we built a multilingual state infrastructure for civic participation.”
The group worked with lawmakers to introduce House Bill 835, “Learning AAPI Contributions in Schools.” This legislation would ensure the inclusion of the contributions of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders in the American history curriculum, like their work on the transcontinental railroad and Civil Rights Movement. 
AAPI advocates, lawmakers promote election reforms, voting rights, DEI at Raleigh lobby day

There’s been traction at the local level, Rep. Ya Liu (D-Wake) said. 
“In one of the high schools in my district, Green Hope High School, the history teacher started to teach a course on AAPI history, which is so popular that it will be one of the elective courses in Wake County,” Liu said. “We’ll continue to push it at the state level.”
The bill was introduced in the House last April, but was assigned to the Rules committee, where bills filed by Democrats are often left to languish. 
Lawmakers have also pushed legislation against hate crimes. 
Senate Bill 827, “Hate Crimes Prevention Act,” would establish a statewide database to track statistics on hate crimes, train law enforcement officers to identify and respond to them, and increase the punishment for them. 
Sen. Jay Chaudhuri (D-Wake), a primary sponsor of the bill, said he filed the measure because the current system isn’t working. 
“We lack a comprehensive statewide database tracking hate crimes, which means that we cannot fully see what is happening in our communities,” he said. “Our law enforcement officers often lack the training to identify, respond to and report these crimes. Our prosecutors need better tools to bring these cases to justice, which means too many perpetrators walk away without accountability.”
The bill has been assigned to the Senate Committee on Appropriations/Base Budget.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Legislature sustains Gov. Mills’ veto of bill to automatically seal certain criminal records
description: There was not enough legislative support to override Gov. Janet Mills’ veto of a bipartisan bill to adopt an automatic record sealing system for certain low-level crimes, which would have expanded the current petition-based process.  “The message we received from the governor was not that of a co-equal partner in our Republic form of government,” […]
text:
Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross (D-Cumberland) ahead of a vote to override Gov. Janet Mills' veto of legislation that would automatically seal certain criminal records on April 29, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)There was not enough legislative support to override Gov. Janet Mills’ veto of a bipartisan bill to adopt an automatic record sealing system for certain low-level crimes, which would have expanded the current petition-based process. 
“The message we received from the governor was not that of a co-equal partner in our Republic form of government,” bill sponsor Sen. Rachel Talbot Ross (D-Cumberland) said on the floor Wednesday. 
Like other proponents, Talbot Ross said the governor’s explanation for her rejection of the bill was “full of misinformation.”
The Maine Senate voted 20-11, with independent Sen. Rick Bennett of Oxford joining Democrats, falling shy of the two-thirds support needed to overturn the veto. 
Those votes — as well as a similar negative outcome for a temporary ban on data centers — solidify the record of the Legislature failing to override any of Mills’ vetoes during her two terms as governor. 
Supporters put forth the record sealing proposal with the aim to remove barriers to education, housing and employment once people have served their time. This type of change is often called a “clean slate” initiative.
Gov. Mills vetoes legislation to automatically seal certain criminal records

“To me, this is a no-brainer,” said Tess Parks, policy director for the Maine Recovery Access Project (ME-RAP), a statewide organization focused on community and policy-based solutions to addiction. “This veto was senseless.” 
The current process, which requires someone to petition the court to seal their conviction if they meet the legal requirements, is rarely used. Supporters say an automatic process would remove barriers, such as needing the time and knowledge to navigate the system on one’s own or hire an attorney to assist.
Data shows that there’s been some increased use of the petition-based system since the state expanded eligibility in 2024 and began more clearly highlighting the process on the judicial branch website, though fewer people are still requesting records to be sealed than are eligible.  
In 2023, 14 petitions for record sealing were filed statewide and eight were granted. In 2025, 173 petitions were filed and 49 were granted. The automatic sealing bill, as amended, was estimated to impact about 123,000 people. 
Since the bill’s public hearing in January, advocacy organizations, formerly incarcerated people, prosecutors, business and others worked with lawmakers to find a version of the proposal everyone could support. The version they settled on — and the Maine Legislature passed with bipartisan support — would have automatically sealed a subset of misdemeanor offenses for people who have completed their sentence and remained crime-free, far fewer crimes than initially proposed. 
The legislation excluded certain offenses from eligibility for sealing, such as assault and sex crimes. In her veto message on Friday, Mills pointed out that Class D crimes for domestic violence assault were not among the ineligible offenses. 
But, those behind the bill said that omission was a clerical drafting error that would have been fixed before implementation, which would not have been until 2028. 
“Without doubting the seriousness of this error,” Talbot Ross said, “we all know that such errors occur frequently and are a part of every legislative process. This is so commonplace that we have an annual bill that corrects such errors across many pieces of legislation,” referring to what’s called the “errors bill.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
The governor’s other objections have been recurring concerns held by opponents to an automatic sealing process over recent years: cost and constitutionality.  
Mills pointed out the bill’s more than $1 million annual price tag, mostly for new hires. But lawmakers defending the legislation in floor speeches argued it would eventually be much less expensive for the state, as the goal is for it to be an automatic, electronic process. 
Mills also argued automatic sealing would violate the right of the public to access records of criminal proceedings under the First Amendment — sharing that concern with the Maine Press Association, Maine Freedom of Information Coalition and New England First Amendment Coalition. 
Mills and those groups point to a ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit that suggests that categorically sealing criminal records without conducting a case-by-case review of the circumstances violates the First Amendment. But proponents of the legislation argue versions of automatic sealing have already been adopted by 13 other states and U.S. territories. 
“Those are non-reasons,” Sen. Mark Lawrence (D-York) said of the cost and constitutionality concerns. 
Opponents won out this year, though it is not the end of efforts to get a “clean slate” law in Maine.
“There is a commitment to working in a future Legislature on bringing this proposal back,” Parks said. “A lot of the groundwork, momentum and excitement for this has been growing.”
Editor’s Note: Maine Press Association represents about 50 newspapers and digital news outlets in the state, including Maine Morning Star.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Buttigieg endorses Montana Plan, announces Butte town hall
description: Transparent Election Initiative announced this week that former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg has endorsed the “Montana Plan” which seeks to keep corporate money out of politics through a ballot measure. Buttigieg will come to Butte for a town hall on May 17, the release from the Transparent Election Initiative said. The event will […]
text:
U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg speaks on night three of the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Ill., on Aug. 21, 2024. (Photo by Andrew Roth | Michigan Advance)Transparent Election Initiative announced this week that former U.S. Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg has endorsed the “Montana Plan” which seeks to keep corporate money out of politics through a ballot measure.
Buttigieg will come to Butte for a town hall on May 17, the release from the Transparent Election Initiative said. The event will start at 1 p.m. and the location will be announced later, the release said.
Initiative I-194 needs 30,000 signatures by June 19 to be on the November ballot. It started as a state Constitutional initiative, but now is a statutory initiative, which would change Montana state law – not the Constitution.
The initiative would create a new law to prohibit corporations, which are known in law as “artificial persons,” from spending money on political candidates or ballot issues in the state. It’s a direct challenge to the federal Citizens United ruling, a case where the U.S. Supreme Court said the power to spend money in elections is tantamount to free speech.
“Montana has a history, going back to the days of the Copper Kings, of dealing with and standing up to concentrated power and wealth, distorting democracy, and the Montana Plan is a way to change all of that under our Constitution and under the legal system that already exists, to change the trajectory of politics by making sure that there isn’t that kind of corporate spending,” Buttigieg said in a video accompanying the release. “The basic principle is simple, that no corporation or any other kind of outside group should be able to distort decision making with massive wealth and dark money.”
Butte was chosen intentionally for the event, harkening to its important place in the country’s labor movement and what can happen when power, money, and politics become deeply intermixed.
“There is no more fitting place than Butte to have this conversation,” Jeﬀ Mangan, former Montana Commissioner of Political Practices and founder of the Transparent Election Initiative said in a release. “Montanans know what happens when economic power becomes political power. From the Copper Kings to the Anaconda Company, Butte has lived through what it means when elections answer to corporations instead of citizens.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: On Law Day, SC attorneys will become teachers about legal career possibilities
description: The first thing that often comes to mind when people think of a legal career is a character they have seen on TV dramas like “Law & Order” or those featured in a John Grisham novel or movie. This week, we recognize Community Law Week, and, as a practicing attorney, I want to use this […]
text:
Phylicia Coleman reads to students on Law Day 2025 at Lonnie B. Elementary School in Columbia, South Carolina. (Photo courtesy of Phylicia Coleman)    The first thing that often comes to mind when people think of a legal career is a character they have seen on TV dramas like “Law & Order” or those featured in a John Grisham novel or movie.
This week, we recognize Community Law Week, and, as a practicing attorney, I want to use this opportunity to help people understand that there are so many other roles lawyers play that don’t involve high-profile court cases and so many ways to find your place in this profession.
Like so many of my colleagues, my journey to becoming a lawyer wasn’t the fulfillment of my childhood dream.
From the age of 7, when the inevitable question was asked — what do you want to be when you grow up — my answer was always a teacher.
To me, that was the logical path for someone who wanted to be in front of a group of people talking about a subject I loved.
Fast forward seven years, and my plans changed dramatically — or so I thought. As a 14-year-old high school freshman, I decided that law school was the direction I was headed. But I knew I wanted a more non-traditional role.
In law school, I found my passion for compliance and contracts.
For fun, I read contracts to identify important clauses and sought to understand why they were phrased in a particular way. As a professional, I took great pride in reading and applying policies in ways that would benefit businesses and individuals.
This was my way of becoming the teacher I thought I wanted to be long ago.
My clients became employees of agencies, the community, and student-athletes. My curriculum was state laws, federal regulations, ethics rules and NCAA rules. My classroom was a conference table, telephone calls, and Microsoft Teams meetings.
But the mission was the same: to help people become more educated and successful.
On May 1, nationally recognized as Law Day, I get to take my expertise to a real classroom.
As part of this SC Bar celebration, my colleagues in the Young Lawyers Division and I will be going into schools around the state to educate students about the legal profession.
Forty-eight teachers from Walterboro to Westminster have invited us to read books about being a lawyer to elementary school students and answer questions from older students about what it is like to have a career in law. This year, I have the pleasure of visiting Meadow Glenn Middle School in Lexington.
This day of recognition and education began at the American Bar Association back in 1957, nearly 60 years ago.
Today, Law Day provides the South Carolina Bar, made up of more than 19,000 members, the opportunity to remind our neighbors and communities of our mission to promote high-quality legal education and to continually improve the administration of justice in the Palmetto State.
Just as my career ambitions evolved, the legal profession has grown and changed since the inception of Law Day. It is my hope, as a lawyer-educator, that I can help grow the appreciation of and pursuit of the wide-ranging careers in America’s unique legal system.
Our judicial branch is designed to uphold order, deliver justice, and protect individual rights with the goal of protecting a stable and fair society. To me, a career in our legal system is a noble pursuit and one I encourage others to consider.

name: Delaware
title: Firearm Bill to Place Expanded Requirements on Dealers, Appears to Establish Registry
description: Supporters cite safety, critics warn of costs and data collection A bill being prepared in Delaware would create a new state-level licensing and oversight program for firearm dealers, layering additional requirements on top of the federal firearms license (FFL) system. The bill is being prepared by Democratic Senator David Sokola (Senate Pro Tempore – repres[...]
text:
Legislative Hall, Dover, Delaware
Supporters cite safety, critics warn of costs and data collection
Senate President Pro Tempore, David Sokola (SD8)
A bill being prepared in Delaware would create a new state-level licensing and oversight program for firearm dealers, layering additional requirements on top of the federal firearms license (FFL) system. The bill is being prepared by Democratic Senator David Sokola (Senate Pro Tempore – representing SD8).  Backers say the proposal would strengthen accountability and reduce theft and illegal diversion, while opponents argue it duplicates federal regulation, threatens small businesses and could function as a de facto firearm registry.  Similar legislation has originated with “Brady – United Against Gun Violence” organization in California, Colorado, Washington (state) and Illinois.
What the bill would do
The proposal would replace Delaware’s existing “deadly weapons dealer” license with a new state firearm dealer license, applying to anyone who sells more than 10 firearms in a 12‑month period. Dealers would need to hold both the federal FFL and the new state license, and would face additional requirements for background checks, security, recordkeeping and reporting.

State licensing and renewals: fingerprint-based state and FBI background checks for dealers and other “responsible persons,” including at renewal.
Security: alarm systems and digital surveillance covering entrances, exits, storage and firearm-handling areas; video retention requirements, with reduced standards for smaller or home-based dealers.
Records and reporting: acquisition/disposition logs, periodic inventory checks, retention of transaction and trace-related records, and required submissions to state regulators.
Insurance: a requirement that dealers carry $1 million in liability coverage.
Training: a state-created or approved course on topics including straw purchasing, trafficking indicators, theft prevention, and recognizing potential suicide risk.

Supporters’ case: tighter oversight and theft prevention
Supporters of the measure, including gun-safety advocates, including Brady – United Against Gun Violence and Moms Demand Action Against Gun Violence, argue that the state should set clearer baseline rules for firearm commerce beyond federal minimums. They say mandatory alarms and cameras would help deter burglaries and reduce the number of stolen guns that later turn up in crimes. Backers also contend that stronger recordkeeping and reporting can help investigators spot trafficking patterns and identify dealers who repeatedly show up in trace requests.
On concerns about a registry, supporters generally respond that the bill regulates dealers rather than individual gun owners, and that many core records already exist under federal law. They frame the additional state reporting as a tool for compliance and enforcement rather than a system intended to track lawful owners.
Opponents’ case: duplication, cost burdens and privacy fears
Critics argue the bill creates a parallel state licensing structure on top of the federal FFL system, adding fees, inspections and paperwork without clear evidence it would reduce violent crime. They also warn that requirements for surveillance equipment, long-term video storage, and $1 million in liability insurance could be manageable for large retailers but prohibitively expensive for small or home-based dealers, potentially pushing some out of business and reducing consumer options.
Opponents also say that periodic submission of acquisition and disposition records to the state could give officials detailed visibility into firearm transactions and amount to a de facto registry even if the word “registry” never appears in the bill. With the requirement for semi-annual reporting of firearm transactions to the state, these records become subject to Freedom of Information Act requests from the public.  Currently, records are held exclusively by the firearms dealer and available for use by law enforcement for tracing purposes, but not subject to public access. Note that the proposed bill explicitly repeals existing Delaware law that prohibits the creation of a firearm registry (Title 24, Chapter 9). Some critics further argue that raising the cost of legal sales could push more transfers into informal channels or out-of-state markets.
Cost and capacity questions
In an analysis performed by (Delaware State Sportsmen’s Association president and firearms-rights advocate) Jeff Hague, he said the program is designed to be sustained by dealer fees and estimated its cost at $3.6 million annually. Using an asserted statewide sales pace of roughly 43,000 firearms per year, the analysis calculates an added cost of about $84 per firearm sold. He noted that overall firearm sales fell about 50% after Delaware’s “permit to purchase” law took effect, and that handgun sales have declined about 80%.  This is clearly an effort to drive firearms dealers out of business and reduce access to legally acquired firearms.
Opponents also point to Delaware’s ongoing effort to stand up the Firearm Transaction Approval Program (FTAP), a state background-check management system approved in 2022, as a sign the state may struggle to administer a new dealer-licensing program. The FTAP process represented a bipartisan effort to improve the quality and effectiveness of criminal background checks for firearms purchases. Delaware has invested $10 million toward FTAP, but the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives has deemed the process “non-compliant,” requiring continued use of the federal National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS). Supporters of FTAP, including some backers of expanded oversight, have argued the system could improve how protection-from-abuse orders and certain state mental health information are reflected in background-check decisions.
Debate over how crime guns are sourced
Critics of the proposal cite statistics they say show only a small share of guns used in crimes are directly purchased from a licensed dealer, with one survey cited in their materials putting the figure at 1.2%. They also note that while many guns traced by ATF can be linked back to a licensed dealer as the first retail point of sale, they may have later moved through theft, illegal purchase or unlawful transfer. Supporters counter that those pathways—especially theft and straw purchasing—are precisely why dealer security, training and tighter oversight could matter, even if the original sale was legal.
What happens next
The proposal is still being prepared, and details such as fee levels, reporting formats and enforcement mechanisms could change as legislative language is finalized. If introduced, the bill would be expected to receive committee hearings where dealer groups, law enforcement, gun-violence prevention organizations and civil-liberties advocates could seek changes before any floor votes.
What is a “Firearm Registry?”
A firearm registry is a government database that records details about legally owned firearms, such as the owner’s name, address, firearm type, make, model, and serial number. Proponents argue it promotes accountability and aids law enforcement; opponents view it as a tool for excessive government oversight of a constitutional right.
Potential Benefits (Pro-Registration Arguments)
Advocates, including gun violence prevention groups, claim registries can:

Help trace crime guns: By linking recovered firearms to their last known legal owner, police can investigate straw purchases, trafficking, or prohibited possessors more efficiently. Some studies on related policies (like handgun licensing or dealer record-keeping in states such as California) suggest they reduce the share of crime guns originating from in-state retail sources.
Support enforcement of prohibitions: When someone becomes a prohibited person (e.g., due to a domestic violence conviction or mental health adjudication), a registry could help identify and require surrender of their firearms.
Officer safety: Dispatchers could alert responding officers to the presence and type of registered firearms at an address.
Accountability for owners: It may deter negligent transfers or encourage secure storage, though evidence here is indirect.

Concerns and Risks (Anti-Registration Arguments)
Critics, including many gun rights organizations and Second Amendment advocates, highlight several practical and philosophical problems:

Ineffectiveness against criminals: Law-abiding owners comply with registration; criminals and those acquiring guns illegally (via theft, black market, or straw purchases) generally do not. A registry thus creates a list of compliant citizens while doing little to disarm threats. CDC reviews and other analyses have found limited or no clear evidence that registration itself reduces overall violent crime rates.
Privacy and data security: Registries compile sensitive personal information tied to a fundamental right. Data breaches have occurred (e.g., in California and Canada), potentially exposing gun owners to burglary, identity theft, or harassment. A centralized list also raises risks of misuse by future administrations or hackers.
Government control and slippery slope: Registration makes future restrictions easier to enforce. Historical examples include:

New York City: Used its long-gun registry (enacted 1967) in the 1990s to enforce bans on certain semiautomatic rifles and shotguns, requiring surrender or rendering inoperable.
Other cases: Registries in places like Nazi Germany, Soviet regimes, and some modern contexts facilitated confiscations after political shifts (though causation and context are debated). In the U.S., post-Hurricane Katrina incidents in New Orleans involved temporary seizures from registered or visible firearms.
Broader pattern: Once a government knows exactly who owns what and where, policy changes (bans on certain firearm types, “assault weapon” restrictions, or broader measures) become administratively simpler.


Compliance burden and chilling effect: Paperwork, fees, and fear of future targeting can deter lawful ownership, especially for self-defense or in high-crime areas. Federal law (Firearms Owners’ Protection Act of 1986 and Brady Act provisions) explicitly prohibits a national firearms registry to prevent this centralized power.
No strong crime reduction link: U.S. violent crime and murder rates fell dramatically from the early 1990s peak through the 2010s in a period without a national registry and with many states prohibiting or limiting them.

Current U.S. Landscape

No comprehensive national firearm registry exists by statute. The ATF maintains records from Federal Firearms Licensees (FFLs) on sales, but these are decentralized and not designed as an owner registry (though concerns exist about digitization and potential backdoors).
A handful of states (e.g., Hawaii, D.C. for all firearms; others for handguns or “assault weapons”) have registration requirements. Several states explicitly ban state-level registries.
Related policies like universal background checks or permit systems are more common and sometimes conflated with full registration.

Broader Implications
A registry shifts the default from “rights-respecting with targeted prohibitions” toward treating firearm ownership as a heavily administered privilege. It increases administrative state power over a right explicitly protected by the Second Amendment (as interpreted in cases like District of Columbia v. Heller and Bruen). For those concerned about government overreach, the core issue is not current benign intent but the infrastructure it creates for future politicians or bureaucrats—especially amid polarized debates over “assault weapons,” red-flag laws, or confiscation proposals.
Evidence on effectiveness remains contested: Supporters cite correlations in strict-licensing states; opponents note that criminals bypass legal channels and that overall U.S. trends show crime declines without nationwide registration. Data security failures and historical enforcement examples fuel distrust.
In short, while a registry might offer marginal investigative tools in ideal conditions, it primarily burdens and monitors the law-abiding population, creates enduring privacy vulnerabilities, and lowers barriers to more restrictive policies. The debate ultimately hinges on whether one trusts government competence and restraint with such lists more than the risks of non-compliance by bad actors.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico House commission hires Albuquerque firm in Epstein probe
description: The New Mexico House 'truth commission' tasked to examine the activities of late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s activity at his Santa Fe County Zorro Ranch property has hired an Albuquerque law firm to help with the investigation.
text:
Maps of the Zorro Ranch from a New Mexico State Land Trust file and photos of the Santa Fe County residence once owned by convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Graphics courtesy of State Land Office/U.S. Department of Justice)The bipartisan New Mexico House investigatory subcommittee tasked with documenting the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein’s activity at his Santa Fe County Zorro Ranch property has hired an Albuquerque law firm to assist in the investigation.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX
The committee on Tuesday announced the appointment of Fadduol, Cluff, Hardy & Conaway, P.C., a law firm with offices in both New Mexico and Texas, to serve as the special counsel. According to the state’s request for proposals for the work, the firm will provide legal services for the commission, gather evidence for its Epstein investigation and manage any collaborations with the New Mexico Department of Justice.
Shawna Casebier, the director of the Legislative Counsel Service, told Source NM Wednesday that 10 firms sought the contract for the subcommittee. The contract caps payments to the law firm for its services at $750,000.
In a news release, the commission said the appointment of special counsel ensures that investigation will be “thorough, transparent and legally sound,” and that public meetings will be scheduled later in the year.
“The Truth Commission has a responsibility to pursue the facts with care and credibility,” subcommittee chair state Rep. Andrea Romero (D-Santa Fe) said in a statement. “Engaging experienced legal counsel ensures that our work is conducted with the rigor and independence necessary to build public trust and deliver meaningful accountability.”
The subcommittee was established unanimously by the New Mexico House in the most recent legislative session. It has a budget of $2 million from a 2023 settlement with the state and several financial services companies for failing to identify the abuses at the ranch.
Attorney Joshua Conaway, a partner at the firm with more than two decades of experience, said in a statement the subcommittee’s work “is both significant and sensitive, and we are committed to helping ensure that its efforts are conducted with integrity, diligence, and respect for all involved.”
A call to Conaway Wednesday was not immediately returned.
In February, NMDOJ announced it was reviving an investigation into Epstein and Zorro Ranch. Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas previously told Source NM his office was investigating Epstein until federal prosecutors in 2019 asked him to shelve the query. Earlier this month, NMDOJ investigators searched the sprawling 7,500-acre property that Epstein bought from former New Mexico Gov. Bruce King in the 1990s.
The commission is scheduled to make an interim report on the investigation to the House of Representatives by July 31, and a final report by the end of 2026.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Records show Ted Carter tried to get podcaster an NU job during his tenure
authors: Jolie Peal, Nebraska Public Media News
description: Former University of Nebraska President Ted Carter tried to get a job at NU for a woman he later admitted he was having an “inappropriate relationship” with, according to a records request obtained Wednesday by Nebraska Public Media News. Carter last month resigned from his position as Ohio State University president, which he had held […]
text:
Ted Carter, then-president of the University of Nebraska system, testifies at the Nebraska Legislature. (Todd Gottula/University of Nebraska at Kearney)Former University of Nebraska President Ted Carter tried to get a job at NU for a woman he later admitted he was having an “inappropriate relationship” with, according to a records request obtained Wednesday by Nebraska Public Media News.
Carter last month resigned from his position as Ohio State University president, which he had held since January 2024, because of “an inappropriate relationship with someone seeking public resources to support her personal business.” Carter abruptly left for OSU after leading NU from 2020 to 2023.
Records made available by NU show that in April 2023, Carter requested the same woman, who has been identified as podcaster Krisanthe Vlachos, be considered for a position at the National Strategic Research Institute, which operates for the NU system in Omaha. University leaders told Nebraska Public Media News last week that they would review internal records after the OSU report was published.
NU emails show Carter sent Vlachos’ resume to Rick Evans, executive director of the National Strategic Research Institute and a retired major general in the U.S. Air Force. Evans responded, saying “her skills are probably best aligned to the Contracts and Business Operations Coordinator position you approved us to hire.”
He went on to say the position would be based in Omaha, and thanked Carter for the tip. Carter responded that he believed Vlachos “is more than willing to relocate to Omaha.” It’s not known if Vlachos was ever considered for that job or any other one at NU.
The next time there was email communication between Carter and Vlachos via the university email system was July 2023. It was a quick note from Carter saying, “Sorry to be out of touch for a bit. He then gave his phone number, which was redacted.
Nebraska Public Media News reached out to NU officials and Regent Chairman Paul Kenney for comment but has not received responses.
Carter appeared to have first met Vlachos while at NU during a Veterans in Energy forum in Washington, D.C. in March 2023, the OSU report said. The report further details that while at OSU, Vlachos had “extraordinary access” to Carter, including at least 24 meetings with him and five trips together.
The report also said at least 14 OSU employees received direct requests from Carter to assist Vlachos. One employee who did help was Chris Kabourek, former NU chief financial officer and former NU interim president.
Kabourek had left NU for Ohio State in the fall of 2024. Kabourek resigned earlier this month and has since been hired as vice president and chief financial officer at West Virginia University.

name: Mississippi Today
title: US Supreme Court Callais decision just weakened the Voting Rights Act. What happens next in Mississippi?
description: A three-judge panel of the Mississippi Supreme Court listens to arguments over a state law that would put $10 million of federal pandemic relief money into infrastructure grants for private schools, Tuesday, Feb. 6, 2024, in Jackson, Miss. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
text:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story.
ABERDEEN — A federal judge in Mississippi will soon decide if she should go forward with adopting a new Mississippi Supreme Court district map now that the nation’s highest court has significantly weakened the federal Voting Rights Act. 
Mississippi Republican Gov. Tate Reeves, at the same time, wants lawmakers to create new state Supreme Court election maps, in a special session of the Legislature he has ordered to happen May 20, now that the U.S. high court has ruled in a landmark Louisiana v. Callais redistricting case.
Also, politicians in Mississippi and across the South are pondering whether the U.S. Supreme Court ruling will allow them to redraw lines along party affiliation for this year’s midterms now that racial safeguards appear to have been weakened. That might prove a difficult task in Mississippi, since it has already held midterm congressional primaries and its congressional lines already greatly favor the GOP, which holds all but one of six congressional seats.
But Mississippi is set to deal with state Supreme Court districts in the short term.
Senior U.S. District Judge Sharion Aycock held a hearing Tuesday in Aberdeen, weighing whether she should quickly craft a new map for at least some of the state judges to run in possible November special elections or wait for guidance from the nation’s highest court. 
“It is a balancing act,” Aycock said. 
But now that guidance has arrived. 
The U.S. Supreme Court on Wednesday, a day after Aycock’s hearing in northeast Mississippi, struck down Louisiana’s second majority Black congressional district in a decision that could open the door for Republican-led states to eliminate Black and Latino electoral districts that tend to favor Democrats and affect the balance of power in Congress.
“That map is an unconstitutional gerrymander,” Justice Samuel Alito wrote for the six conservatives.
The court’s conservative majority found that the district relied too heavily on race and weakened the landmark voting rights law’s protections against discrimination in redistricting.
But the Mississippi case involves three Mississippi Supreme Court districts and is different from the Louisiana congressional district case, something that Aycock acknowledged during Tuesday’s hearing. 
“I do think they’re very different cases,” Aycock told attorneys. 
Judge Sharion Aycock
The Mississippi litigation started in April 2022 when the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Mississippi, the Southern Poverty Law Center and private law firms, on behalf of a group of Black Mississippians, sued the state because they believed Black voters in certain parts of the state couldn’t elect a candidate of their choice.  
Aycock ruled in August 2025 that the districts illegally dilute Black strength and needed to be redrawn. She allowed the Legislature to come up with a new map during its 2026 session earlier this year, but it declined to do so. 
Aycock justified the ruling by noting that no Black person has ever been elected to the Mississippi Supreme Court without having first obtained an interim appointment from the governor. 
But the conservative Mississippi Legislature was unpersuaded. Since the lawmakers didn’t adopt new maps, attorneys were back in court on Tuesday to argue about how the judge should proceed. 
The plaintiffs proposed three different redrawn maps for consideration, while state officials asked Aycock not to adopt any map until the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais decision
Ari Savitzky is an attorney for the plaintiffs, and he argued that Aycock should move forward quickly with adopting a new map to prevent Black votes from being diluted any longer. 
“The remedy must end vote dilution by increasing political opportunity for Black voters,”  Savitzky said. “That’s the bottom line.” 
Bill Cooper, a redistricting expert for the plaintiffs, created the three new maps that Aycock could implement: one called the race-blind plan, another called the least-change plan and a final one called the regional plan. 
Cooper testified that he did not use racial demographics to craft any of the proposals. Instead, he used data such as sustained poverty rates in certain counties to create a uniform district. 
But Michael Wallace, an outside attorney representing the state, pointed out that a disproportionate number of Black Mississippians are impoverished when compared to white citizens. So he could use poverty as a proxy for racial data.
Wallace also cast doubt that Cooper’s maps could truly be race-neutral because he’s previously done redistricting work in Mississippi. 
“Didn’t you tell the court when you testified here before that you’ve done a lot of work here in Mississippi, so you understand the state by race?” Wallace asked. 
Mississippi Supreme Court races generally receive less voter participation than other races, but the state’s highest court has ruled on several vital issues in recent years, such as the state’s ballot initiative and allowing the Legislature to give money to private schools. 
If Aycock still believes a new map should be implemented after the Callais decision, she could adopt one of the maps the plaintiffs presented, tweak one of the plaintiffs’ maps or employ an outside expert to help her craft a map. 
Another complication for the future of the state Supreme Court’s district lines is how Mississippi politicians respond to the Callais decision. 
Reeves has ordered lawmakers to return to Jackson in three weeks to redraw the state Supreme Court districts, even though those same lawmakers declined to redraw the districts in response to Aycock’s initial order. 
It’s unclear how lawmakers will respond to the Callais case and how Aycock would respond to a potential new map from the Legislature.  
She asked attorneys in court if she should tell the Legislature that she preferred they adopt a certain map or if she should wait for the Legislature to act before she adopts a map. The attorneys responded that Aycock has wide latitude to decide how to proceed. 
Justin Matheny, an attorney with the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office, told Aycock that she should not adopt a map until after the Callais ruling because the Legislature could choose to adopt a competing plan to her plan, which would then likely prompt a new round of litigation. 
“We would be here in three or four months or however long it would be and in an even bigger mess than we’re in right now,” Matheny said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Republican Chas Calenda to remain in charge of U.S. Attorney’s Office for Rhode Island
description: Interim U.S. Attorney Charles “Chas” Calenda’s 120-day term as Rhode Island’s top federal prosecutor expired Tuesday. But he’s still leading the Providence office. Calenda announced Wednesday morning that Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed him as a “Special Attorney” and designated him as First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Rho[...]
text:
After completing his 120-day term as interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Rhode Island, the Trump administration wants Charles C. Calenda to continue to lead the office as a special attorney and first assistant U.S. Attorney. (U.S. Department of Justice)Interim U.S. Attorney Charles “Chas” Calenda’s 120-day term as Rhode Island’s top federal prosecutor expired Tuesday. But he’s still leading the Providence office.
Calenda announced Wednesday morning that Acting U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appointed him as a “Special Attorney” and designated him as First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the District of Rhode Island.
“While my title may have changed, my goals and the mission of this office have not,” Calenda  said in a statement. “We have a great deal of work ahead, and I will remain focused on keeping Rhode Islanders safe and secure from those who wish to do harm.”
Made public Wednesday, the appointment order Blanche submitted April 13 states Calenda will have the authority to perform the duties of the United States attorney for the District of Rhode Island while the position remains vacant, circumventing the traditional nomination process
“Mr. Calenda is likewise authorized to perform all the delegable, nonexclusive functions of the Attorney General in conducting in the District of Rhode Island any kind of legal proceeding, civil or criminal, including grand jury proceedings and proceedings before United States Magistrate Judges,” Blanche wrote. “This authority includes supervising the conduct of Assistant United States Attorneys and Special Assistant United States Attorneys working on such proceedings.”
Dulce Donovan, whom Calenda appointed as first assistant U.S. attorney on March 24, will become executive assistant US attorney. All other supervisory personnel will remain in their same positions with the same titles, according to the U.S. Attorney’s office.
Calenda’s job title update came nearly three hours after Rhode Island’s federal court on Wednesday issued an order stating it would not use its authority to appoint an interim U.S. attorney to replace Calenda.
“This court has carefully considered its power to appoint an interim U.S. Attorney under these factors and concluded that, to continue the uninterrupted and orderly operation of the federal criminal justice system in Rhode Island, and to ensure the non-political professional operation of the U.S. Attorney’s office, at this time it will not exercise its option to make such an appointment,” Chief Judge John J. McConnell Jr. wrote.
Declining to make an appointment avoids a conflict with the Trump administration, which was quick to fire U.S. Attorneys appointed by the courts in other blue states, namely New Jersey, upstate New York, and Virginia.
A search for Calenda’s replacement began with an April 2 call for applications. Six applications were submitted by the April 16 deadline, court spokesperson Frank Perry confirmed in an email to Rhode Island Current.
Under federal law, interim appointments made by the AG serve up to 120 days. If no permanent Senate-confirmed replacement is appointed within that timeframe, the vacancy may be filled by the local federal district court. 
The court may reconsider its determination at any time “should circumstances that underpin these values warrant,” McConnell’s order states. Perry said court officials would likely seek applications again if they were to consider making an appointment.
Calenda, a West Greenwich Republican Town Council member who ran unsuccessfully for state attorney general in 2022, was appointed interim Rhode Island’s top federal prosecutor by then-U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi on Dec. 23, 2025. He was formally sworn in on Dec. 30.
Rhode Island’s junior Democratic U.S. Sheldon Whitehouse, blasted Calenda’s appointment at the time, calling him a “MAGA stooge.” Whitehouse’s office did not immediately respond to request for comment.
Since being appointed last December, Calenda said he has tried to run the office “at the highest levels of efficiency, integrity and professionalism.”
“For however long I serve this District, I will continue to work alongside our federal, state, and local partners for the betterment of our state,” he said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Financial opacity, staff shortages and poor conditions scrutinized in Michigan nursing homes
description: There is an overarching belief that nursing homes are not profitable, members of the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative told the Senate Oversight Committee in a Wednesday morning hearing, but said that sentiment is not always true. Group members told lawmakers that nursing homes have an opaque and complex corporate structure that makes it hard to […]
text:
Getty ImagesThere is an overarching belief that nursing homes are not profitable, members of the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative told the Senate Oversight Committee in a Wednesday morning hearing, but said that sentiment is not always true.
Group members told lawmakers that nursing homes have an opaque and complex corporate structure that makes it hard to track if greater profits are being hidden.
That lack of transparency in the finances of nursing homes, combined with what those testifying called an overall low standard of care at many of these facilities, led the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative to start taking a closer look at what is actually going on behind the scenes in nursing homes — and to urge the Legislature to require greater transparency and oversight. 
“The nursing home industry says there simply isn’t enough money to do better, and that’s where our advocacy has always unfortunately ended,” Alison Hirschel, director of the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative, said in the hearing. “The reason it matters so much is because there are thousands of people across the state, your constituents, who are living in nursing homes and not getting the quality of care of life that you would consider acceptable for yourself or you would want for somebody you care about.”
“What at one point was not acceptable seems to now be acceptable,” Salli Pung, the Michigan long-term care ombudsman, said. “We need to hold providers and the owners accountable to meeting the minimum requirements to afford residents the highest quality of life and their appropriate care.”
Members of the Michigan Elder Justice Initiative testify to the Senate Oversight Committee on conditions at Michigan nursing homes. April 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
Dr. Ashvin Gandhi, professor at the UCLA Anderson School of Management, explained some of the techniques that can be used to hide profits by some nursing home ownership. 
Specifically, Gandhi explained, some nursing home owners use a strategy that he calls “profit tunnelling,” where the same person or group who owns the nursing home will set up a separate real estate holding company and a separate management services company to handle those services for their own nursing home. 
“So on paper, it looks like the nursing homes costs are extremely high relative to the revenues it brings in,” he said. “Observed profits are very low, but then you’re simply booking all of your profits on the real estate company that you set up on paper, or the management company that you set up on paper, or the pharmacy company you set up on paper. And so this ends up looking like the nursing home is extremely unprofitable, when in reality, you are potentially extracting profit through these related parties.”
In Illinois, which has done more than most states in extracting more accurate financial information from nursing homes, operators could make over $1,700 per bed in hidden profits from a real estate company and over $1,400 per bed in a management company.
Pung also described situations in which nursing home residents were not allowed to shower more than once per month or were left stranded in broken mechanical lifts designed to move disabled residents from their wheelchair to a bed or shower. She also showed video clips of a number of nursing home residents describing their circumstances.
Sens. Sam Singh (D-East Lansing) and Mallory McMorrow (D-Royal Oak) react to testimony in the Senate Oversight Committee on conditions at Michigan nursing homes. April 29, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
“It makes me very angry, because we’re supposed to be in a place where we’re supposed to be made comfortable without frustration, without fear,” one resident said in the video. “We want peace, and if we can have that, then we should get it. And we should get it not because somebody is putting our money in their pocket. It should be here at the facility where it’s needed.”
The Michigan Elder Justice Initiative provides services to residents in 427 nursing homes around the state. 
Richie Farran, the executive vice president of government services at the Health Care Association of Michigan, which represents 374 nursing homes, testified to the committee at the end of the hearing to clarify that the association is “not resistant to expanding home- and community-based funding.”
“We’re looking at just a demographic challenge as the demand for care will increase, the caregivers are just not there,” he said. “So providers are doing everything they can to hire as much staff as they can. Quality staff means quality care.”
Farran also added that the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services — which others testifying suggested should be tasked with doing more to scrutinize the finances of nursing homes to avoid “profit tunnelling” — currently has an audit process for nursing facilities and their revenue.

Sunday, May 3, 2026 at 2:00 p.m. Temple Sinai500 Swift St.So. Burlington, VTNo flowers, please.
To join via Zoom: 

Go to https://templesinaivt-org.zoom.us/j/82856204494
Meeting ID: 828 5620 4494
Passcode: Terje


It is with the profound sadness that comes from a sudden and unexpected loss that we share the tragic passing of Terje Anderson. Our beloved brother, uncle, mentor, activist, and dear friend died in a fire at his home in Montgomery, Vermont on March 15, 2026. We take solace in the grace that he passed in the peacefulness of sleep.
To paraphrase a tribute from Dr. Jose Zuniga of the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, Terje was a passionate advocate, a principled leader, a bridge-builder, and a relentless voice for dignity, inclusion and equity.
Born James Terry Anderson on June 29, 1958, in Indiana, PA, his family soon moved to the Baltimore, Maryland area. He was called Jim by his family, but most knew him as Terje, the name he legally adopted as an homage to his Swedish heritage.
Terje attended Randallstown (Maryland) Elementary School, Old Court Junior High, and graduated in 1976 from Randallstown High School where he was captain of their “It’s Academic” high school quiz show, which comes as no surprise to anyone who watched Jeopardy with him.
Terje attended McGill University in Montreal. He became fluent in French, had a solid grasp of Canadian politics, and most importantly, honed a sixth sense of great patisseries and restaurants.
When it came to culinary acumen, Terje was second to none. If he needed inspiration, he turned to his vast collection of cookbooks. By vast, we mean imagine the Library of Congress with Julia Child in charge. A dream day for him would include enjoying a double-shot java from his epic espresso machine, while binge-watching the Great British Baking Show, as he prepared a delicious dinner of the most unique ingredients.
Terje truly enjoyed the communal aspect of sharing meals and discovering new foods. Wherever he lived, he delighted in hosting dinner parties for friends and colleagues. He treasured an annual December tradition of making specialty chocolates with his dear friend Jenn Wallace-Brodeur. The two merry chocolatiers would spend months planning the extravaganza. Gifting those unique and meticulously packaged chocolates to friends and family brought Terje abundant joy. 
If you knew Terje, you knew he loved his dogs beyond measure. Lucy, Rosa and Bronco, each a rescue of sorts, came into his life at different times. Without a doubt, Terje provided them with storybook lives in the Montgomery countryside that other dogs can only dream of. Terje also held a special place in his heart for his dog nieces, Lacey in Virginia and Isla in Burlington.
Terje dedicated his life to social justice and fairness for all. His lived experience as a gay man, when few sexual orientation rights were enshrined in law, drove Terje to commit his professional life and political activism to ensuring people had the agency, freedom, and legal infrastructure to live and love as they want – in peace, in good health, and with acceptance. 
Terje’s public health career focused on HIV and AIDS. In his early years, he worked for the Vermont Department of Health as the AIDS Program Chief. In 1986, along with others caring for friends living with the disease, Terje was instrumental in forming Vermont CARES (Vermont Committee for AIDS Resources, Education and Services). It was the state’s first AIDS service organization, and it grew to meet the unique medical, political, and public perception challenges of the time. 
He later moved to Colorado Springs, where as executive director of the Southern Colorado AIDS Project Terje was appointed to the Governor’s AIDS Council and became a member of the HIV Prevention Community Planning Group. His leadership efforts to advance thoughtful policy were further recognized in 1995 when Terje was appointed by President Bill Clinton to the administration’s Presidential Advisory Council on HIV/AIDS. 
In Washington, DC, Terje served as executive director of the National Association of People with AIDS (NAPWA), advocating for people living with HIV. He traveled throughout the world where he led and participated in conferences, provided education and training, and met with national and international health leaders. Terje said one of the greatest honors of his life was being on the same panel as Coretta Scott King at the U.S. Conference on AIDS, and he spoke emotionally of his meeting Bishop Desmond Tutu.
After a while, the non-stop pace took its toll, and Vermont was calling. Returning to the green mountains, Terje settled in a cozy Montgomery home converted from a one-room schoolhouse surrounded by the beauty of Vermont’s wilderness. He thoroughly enjoyed being part of the Montgomery community and found peace in his life there.
Terje was the consummate political junkie. This passion of his early teens became his vehicle to get in “good trouble” in the interest of a socially just society. At age 14 Terje volunteered for Shirley Chisholm’s historic presidential campaign, and he was a leader of the 1984 Jesse Jackson delegation to the Democratic National Convention. In 1992 he was the first openly gay person in the U.S. to be chair of a national convention state delegation.
There was not a single congressional race Terje didn’t follow, and he could expound on the fortunes of Canadian political parties and global politics. He was a warehouse of electoral data, and reveled in following results late into every election night.
Terje used his understanding of political machinery to truly make a difference. He worked for years in the grassroots trenches doing the hard work of getting out the vote. Terje also knew that both the angels as well as the devil were in the details, and that having a seat at the table was how you throw open the door for everyone whose voice should be heard. 
As a member of the Democratic National Committee and several Presidential Nominating Conventions Platform and Rules Committees, Terje had a direct and meaningful impact on the Democratic Party, building coalitions that helped change party policies and practices to be more progressive, equitable and inclusive. Terje was as fierce in his work for social justice as he was unapologetic in his opposition to authoritarianism and the politics of hate.  
In 2017, Terje became chair of the Vermont Democratic Party where he was a dedicated leader committed to supporting local communities through an engaged electorate.
He immensely enjoyed the honor of being selected one of Vermont’s three members of the Electoral College in the November 2020 election and appeared on live national television as Vermont cast the nation’s first electoral votes to formalize Joe Biden’s victory over Donald Trump.
Terje retired from active politics in 2020 due to complications from multiple sclerosis. He continued to be in close contact with the many people he knew in Vermont and around the world,  and was a regular contributor to online communities.
As his health stabilized, Terje joined the team at Jay Peak Ski Resort. He could be found behind the front desk several days a week, welcoming guests, troubleshooting youth hockey player hijinks, and enjoying time with his new colleagues. He worked at Jay until his passing.
In the thoughtful words of Dr. Zuniga, “Terje’s voice may be gone, but his impact endures in the policies he helped shape, the communities he strengthened, and the lives he influenced.” Simply put, Terje loved his family, his dogs and his friends.
Terje’s family thanks everyone for their many acts of kindness, support and compassion, including the staff and management of Jay Peak Resort, the emergency crews of Franklin and Orleans Counties who responded to the fire, the Vermont State Police, the Health Department’s Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and the family support program of the Northern New England Red Cross. 
Terje was predeceased by his loving parents Max and Barbara Anderson, of Hagerstown, MD; and his adored dogs, Lucy, Rosa and Bronco.
Holding his treasured memory close in their hearts are his beloved sister Kim Anderson Via, of Reston, VA; his nephews, of whom he was so proud, Kevin Via, also of Reston, and Brian Via (Brooke), adored grandniece Lily and grandnephew Caleb, and their sibling whose birth is expected in July, of Herndon, VA; Uncle Butch and Aunt Betty Simpson, of Dubois, PA; Aunt Nancy Anderson, of Creekside, PA.
Terje also leaves behind friends across the globe, including his adopted and cherished Burlington, Vermont family of Ben Truman, Jennifer Wallace-Brodeur, Max, Paul, and their dog Isla – who relished his dog sitting and ball throwing skills.
Keep Terje’s legacy vibrant and alive, be a lifelong voter, and as John Lewis said, get in good trouble. If we all do something, we can change everything.
If you wish to consider a gift in Terje’s memory, may we suggest one of these non-profits:
American Red Cross Northern New England redcross.org/local/me-nh-vt 
Lucy’s House for Prevention of Homeless Pets  Venmo @lucyshouseforpetsvermont (be sure to include “In memory of Terje Anderson” and your address) or mail to the address online under “Get Involved” 
Outright Vermont outrightvt.org
Vermont CARES vtcares.org

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: US Supreme Court strikes down Louisiana congressional maps in case with national implications
description: The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Louisiana’s existing congressional map Wednesday as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander in a ruling that may have implications for core tenets of the Voting Rights Act. “Allowing race to play any part in government decision-making represents a departure from the constitutional rule that applies in almost every other cont[...]
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court has ruled that Louisiana's congressional district map approved in 2024 is an illegal racial gerrymander. (Photo by Wesley Muller/Louisiana Illuminator)The U.S. Supreme Court struck down Louisiana’s existing congressional map Wednesday as an unconstitutional racial gerrymander in a ruling that may have implications for core tenets of the Voting Rights Act. 

“Allowing race to play any part in government decision-making represents a departure from the constitutional rule that applies in almost every other context,” Justice Samuel Alito, who was appointed to the court in 2005 by President George W. Bush, wrote for the majority opinion. “Compliance with Section 2 thus could not justify the state’s use of race-based redistricting here. The state’s attempt to satisfy the Middle District’s ruling, although understandable, was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.”
The decision will not affect the 2026 midterm elections as Louisiana is already too late in the electoral process to adopt new maps. 
While the ruling does not invalidate the Voting Rights Act, it does undermine a legal tool minority voters have used for decades to challenge election maps they believe unfairly dilutes their voting power. 
Conservative justices on the court had previously expressed interest in limiting or banning the consideration of race in the redistricting process.
The three liberal leaning justices dissented from the majority opinion adopted on a 6-3 vote along ideological lines. They accused the majority of dismantling Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits voting laws or procedures that purposefully discriminate on the basis of race, color or membership in a language minority group.
Justice Elena Kagan, who was appointed to the court in 2010 by President Barack Obama wrote “the court’s decision will set back the foundational right Congress granted of racial equality in electoral opportunity.”
The case in question, Callais v. Louisiana, challenges the legality of a second majority-Black congressional district that the Louisiana Legislature, with a Republican majority, drew in 2024. Lawmakers configured that map in response to a federal court ruling over a version of the districts created in 2022 that directed the state to enhance minority voting power based on the Voting Rights Act. Louisiana has six seats in the U.S. House of Representatives, but only one favored a Black candidate before 2024in a state where nearly a third of the population is Black.
This is a developing story
